aAbout: God's Eye View is an open-source 3D world globe simulator — 'a spy-satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real.' It renders Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles through Cesium and layers live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic and public cameras from open sources, all processed locally in your browser. It went viral in 2026 (#1 on GitHub Trending, 61,000+ stars) for its voice-controlled AI agent, cockpit view and sensor-style visual modes. It is software you run yourself — via Pinokio one-click, a terminal install, or Docker — not a website you open.

aLink.label: WorldEye: the God's Eye View alternative

aStrengths: God's Eye View is the more spectacular and the more ownable tool: a photorealistic 3D globe with cockpit view, 3D aircraft models, sensor looks (FLIR, night vision) and a scene director for cinematic tours — all free, all running on your machine with data you can inspect, extend and keep. Its voice agent genuinely has no equivalent here: you talk to the globe and it flies, tracks and annotates. For creators, tinkerers and anyone who wants the globe itself to be the experience, nothing hosted matches it.
bAbout: Argos Atlas is a hosted real-time world map that aggregates already-open official feeds — above all public cameras, which it claims number over 200,000 from official portals in more than 190 countries — and paints everything that moves around them on one flat map: flights, ships, war frontlines, verified events, infrastructure, earthquakes, fires and prediction markets. The live map is free with a free account; ARGOS PRO adds recording, history, an AI analyst layer and a 3D globe mode.
bStrengths: Argos Atlas is the deeper working atlas: an order of magnitude more cameras (its claim), camera recording with a 24-hour scrubbable archive, flight and ship history (7–90 days), sanctions and dark-vessel flags, verified frontlines and events, geofence alerts and a 16-camera videowall. It asks nothing of your computer — a free account in any browser — and its team plans (up to 10 seats on DIVISION) aim it at newsrooms and analysts, not just the curious.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. God's Eye View is a free, open-source 3D globe you run on your own computer — unmatched for immersion, voice control and hackability, with a modest camera layer (~4,000). Argos Atlas is a hosted service built around camera scale (200,000+ claimed), recording, history and verification layers, free to open and paid to remember. If you want to *experience* the planet, install God's Eye View; if you want to *monitor* it from any browser, open Argos Atlas.
consA: You must install and run it yourself (Pinokio, terminal or Docker)
Camera layer is small (~4,000) beside hosted atlases
Ships need a free third-party key; voice spends your OpenAI credit
No recording, no alerts, no hosted sharing for a team
consB: Account required before the map opens; free tier has ads and camera limits
The 3D globe, AI and recording are all paywalled (DISTRICT+)
Export and the camera API are still marked 'coming soon'
Priced in euros with launch discounts — list prices are much higher

faqs.a: No — they are unrelated products. God's Eye View is free open-source software by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis that you install and run locally. Argos Atlas is a hosted website. They share a genre — live world maps — and little else.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View the same as Argos Atlas?

faqs.a: Yes. The software is free and open source under the MIT licence. The only costs are optional third-party ones you control: the voice agent uses your own OpenAI API credit (the app warns at $2 and caps at $5 per session), and photoreal 3D tiles can be metered if you use a direct Google key instead of the free Cesium ion route.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View really free?

faqs.a: Argos Atlas, by its own figures: it claims 200,000+ public cameras in 190+ countries. God's Eye View's CCTV Mesh layer states a shared cap of about 4,000 cameras, projected into its 3D scene. For comparison, WorldEye's directory lists 74,229 public cameras.
faqs.q: Which has more live cameras, God's Eye View or Argos Atlas?

faqs.a: No. Argos Atlas runs in the browser; it asks you to create a free account (Google or an email link). God's Eye View is the opposite: no account at all, but you install it on your own computer first.
faqs.q: Do I need to install anything for Argos Atlas?

faqs.a: Yes, but it's a paid feature: the 3D globe (relief, satellite imagery, 3D aircraft, first-person views) starts at the DISTRICT plan. The free tier is the flat map. God's Eye View's photoreal 3D globe is its core, free interface.
faqs.q: Does Argos Atlas have a 3D globe?

faqs.a: Only Argos Atlas. From DISTRICT it records 15 cameras (150 on DIVISION) with a 24-hour scrubbable archive and downloadable clips. God's Eye View is a live viewer — when it's gone, it's gone.

intro: God's Eye View and Argos Atlas are the two names behind most viral 'watch the whole world live' clips — and they could hardly be built more differently. God's Eye View is free, open-source software (by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis) that you install on your own computer: a photorealistic 3D globe with live flights, ships, satellites and cameras, driven by voice. Argos Atlas is a hosted website that asks only for a free account: a flat live map claiming 200,000+ public cameras, frontlines, verified events and prediction markets, with a paid Pro tier for recording and history.
pricingA: There is no God's Eye View price or subscription — the software is free and open source. The README's own cost table is honest about the edges: most layers cost $0 with no signup; a free-key tier (AISStream, NASA FIRMS, Cesium ion within quota) unlocks more; the voice agent spends your own OpenAI credit with a $2 warning and $5 hard cap per session; and photoreal tiles through a direct Google key are metered by Google.
pricingB: The live atlas is free and, in Argos's words, 'will stay free' — it asks for a free account and shows ads with camera limits. ARGOS PRO (EUR, VAT included in the EU/UK) lists OUTPOST at €15.99/month or €44.99 for 12 months, DISTRICT at €56.99/month or €134.99 for 12 months, DIVISION at €199/month or €809 for 12 months, and AGENCY at €1,049.99/month for registered companies. First-month welcome discounts apply to OUTPOST and DISTRICT; there is no free trial.
prosA: Completely free and open source (MIT) — no subscription, ever
Photorealistic 3D globe with cockpit view and 3D aircraft models

verdictA: Choose God's Eye View if you want the globe as an experience — photoreal 3D, voice control, cockpit rides — you're comfortable installing software, and you want it free and open forever.
verdictB: Choose Argos Atlas if you want a ready-to-open working map with the biggest camera catalogue, recording, history and alerts — and you're willing to pay for the memory features.
verdictLine: God's Eye View is the spectacle — a photoreal 3D globe you own and can extend. Argos Atlas is the workhorse — a hosted camera-first atlas that records what it sees. The first is free software; the second is a free website with paid memory.
worldEye: If installing software is the dealbreaker in God's Eye View, and Argos's account wall and ads are the friction there, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries, live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. It doesn't record cameras like Argos or render photoreal 3D tiles like God's Eye View, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) buys an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than camera archives.
